content.p: On Sunday 14 December 2025 two gunmen opened fire on the Chanukah by the Sea festival in Archer Park at Bondi Beach in Sydney. Fifteen people were killed and dozens more were wounded. It was Australia's deadliest mass shooting in about three decades, and police described it as a terrorist attack inspired by Islamic State. One of the two gunmen, 50-year-old Sajid Akram, died in the confrontation with police. His 24-year-old son, Naveed Akram, was shot, survived and is the surviving gunman. He is accused of 15 murders, 40 attempted murders and committing a terrorist act, among other offences. He has not been required to plead, and as of the latest court reports he remains in custody awaiting the preparation of the prosecution's case.

The festival was in its 31st year, ABC reported. The lighting of the Hanukkah candles in the park is especially popular with families and young children, and the event was organised by Rabbi Eli Schlanger, 41, an assistant rabbi at Chabad-Lubavitch of Bondi, according to NPR. He was among the dead. Al Jazeera reported funerals for Schlanger and Rabbi Yaakov Levitan.

ABC's analysis of more than 80 videos from the scene found that the earliest publicly available footage of the gunmen shows two passers-by, Boris and Sofia Gurman, intervening at about 6:42 p.m. Boris Gurman managed to wrestle a weapon from Sajid Akram, and both Gurmans were shot and killed soon afterwards. Albanese called the couple, both in their 60s, "Australian heroes". Naveed Akram was already firing from the footbridge beside the park, the footage suggested.

According to a police statement of alleged facts released by a Sydney court, the pair parked on Campbell Parade at about 6:50 p.m. and placed Islamic State flags on the windscreens. The document alleges that they then took firearms and homemade explosive devices from the car. Four of the devices were thrown toward the crowd, the document says, but did not detonate. Police assessed the devices as viable. The gap between the two times, 6:42 p.m. on video and about 6:50 p.m. in the police document, is not explained in the reports.

ABC's compilation describes the younger gunman firing from the footbridge while his father moved toward the festival's edge. Ahmed al-Ahmed, a 43-year-old Syrian-Australian shop owner, came up behind the older gunman, tackled him and took his weapon. Naveed Akram then ran down the footbridge stairs and fired three shots toward the group. Al-Ahmed was shot several times in the arm. Albanese praised him as "the best of our country", and a public fundraising page for him raised more than 2.3 million Australian dollars, Al Jazeera reported.

Reuven Morrison charged at the older gunman from the park and threw something at him, according to the ABC footage, and the younger gunman fired four shots in his direction. Elsewhere in the park, survivors lay on the ground. A 71-year-old survivor, Eliyahu Ben Zion, filmed as he walked toward the men with nothing to throw. Jessica Rozen, who was pregnant, shielded a child with her own body. ABC called it the most filmed terror attack in Australian history.

Police response is one of the questions the footage reopens. Three independent audio experts told ABC that a gunshot at 6:45:17 p.m. matched a police 9-millimetre handgun. If police fired it, as the experts assumed because the Akrams were not carrying such weapons, the first police shot came about 51 seconds earlier than previously reported and roughly three minutes after the shooting began.

Sajid Akram was an Indian national, and Naveed Akram is an Australian national. Albanese said the older man had been able to get a gun licence and hold six guns, four of them used in the attack, and the attack renewed scrutiny of the country's gun laws. Australia's domestic intelligence agency had investigated Naveed Akram for six months in 2019 over his alleged extremist associations, police said, but concluded he posed no threat. AFP reported that he slipped off the radar after the agency decided he posed no imminent threat.

Investigators examined a trip the pair made to the southern Philippines in November. The Philippine government said that no evidence had been presented that the men trained there and rejected the description of the country as an Islamic State training ground. Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett said in December that there was no evidence the two were part of a broader terrorist cell or directed by others to carry out the attack.

The statement of alleged facts, released on 22 December in redacted form, accuses the pair of filming themselves firing shotguns at a countryside location in late October, and of recording a video in front of an Islamic State flag in which they allegedly recite political and religious views and summarise their justification for the attack. CCTV footage, it says, shows two men believed to be the Akrams walking along the footbridge on 12 December, which police allege was reconnaissance. These are police allegations, not findings. ABC also noted that Islamic State later claimed the pair as "soldiers", more than ten weeks after the attack.

Naveed Akram was in a coma after the shooting and reportedly woke on the Tuesday after the attack, Al Jazeera said. New South Wales Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said officers had waited until he was able to understand what was happening. On 17 December he was charged with 59 offences. NPR reported that they included a murder charge for each of the 15 deaths, 40 counts of causing harm with intent to murder, one count of committing a terrorist act, and a charge of placing an explosive near a building intending to cause harm. Police said they would allege in court that he engaged in conduct that caused death and serious injury "to advance a religious cause and cause fear in the community". His lawyer did not enter pleas or seek bail at a hospital bedside hearing by video link. Al Jazeera reported that he had so far refused to be interviewed by police.

He was moved from hospital to a correctional facility on 22 December. His first public court appearance was on 16 February 2026, by video link from prison, lasting about five minutes and mostly concerned with suppressing the identities of some victims. According to the AFP report, he said one word, "yeah", when the judge asked whether he had followed a discussion of extending the suppression orders. His lawyer at the time, Ben Archbold, said he was held in "very onerous conditions" and that it was too early to say whether he would plead guilty.

At a hearing in the Downing Centre Local Court in May, a gag order protecting survivors and victims who have not chosen to be identified was discussed, and Akram did not appear on the video screen, Australian Associated Press reported. The Associated Press said court staff told it that 19 more charges had been added to the register on 15 April. On 10 June, ABC reported that the Commonwealth prosecutor told the court that paperwork for 19 additional charges had been filed. They were 10 counts of shooting at with intent to murder, six of discharging a firearm with intent to resist arrest and three of wounding or seriously injuring someone with intent to murder. The prosecutor said the evidence brief contained 230,000 CCTV images and numerous devices from other people reportedly linked to the defendant, and that material required translation. His lawyer, Leonie Gittani, said he had been aware of the possibility of more charges, that the matter was "in its infancy" and that she could not yet enter pleas.

Within days of the attack, Albanese and state leaders said they would tighten the country's gun laws. The federal government announced a gun buyback scheme in December, which AFP described as the largest since 1996, when the Port Arthur massacre killed 35 people. New South Wales Premier Chris Minns recalled parliament to consider capping the number of guns a person may own and reclassifying shotguns, and proposed that no protest applications be accepted after terror events.

Under public pressure from victims' families and others, Albanese announced on 8 January 2026 a federal royal commission led by Virginia Bell, a former High Court judge. Families had written in an open letter asking why "clear warning signs were ignored". The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion is examining intelligence failures, the circumstances of the shooting and the prevalence of antisemitism. A separate review of the security services' response, due in April, was folded into it. ABC reported that public hearings were under way in late February, whereas the Associated Press said in May that the first public hearings began that week. The AP also said an interim report in April urged stricter gun controls. By June ABC reported the commission had been sitting in secret and was due to report by the first anniversary of the attack, 14 December 2026.
